opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The computers we use today, the phone, the laptop, were designed for a world before AI. They assume you go to an app, tap through menus, type into boxes, and do all the orchestration yourself. That made sense when software couldn't understand you.

What we've seen with ChatGPT is that people's behavior has started to shift. They talk to it. They give it context about their lives, ask follow-up questions, and increasingly expect it to just handle things rather than walk them through steps. People aren't using it like a search engine or a tool you pick up and put down. It's more like an ongoing relationship with something that knows what you're working on.

Once you see that, the natural question is whether the current form factors are really the best expression of it. If the AI can understand what you want, maybe you don't need to be staring at a rectangle of glass and pulling things up by hand. Maybe it should be more ambient, more aware of your context, there when you need it and out of the way when you don't.

I don't think the phone goes away anytime soon. It's an incredible device. But I do think there's room for a new kind of computing built from the ground up around the fact that you have this intelligent thing that can help you. The interaction model should come first, and the hardware should follow from that, not the other way around.

The honest answer is that we're still early in figuring out what that looks like. But the way people already use ChatGPT gives us a lot of signal about where it's heading.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT use is changing and that hardware should follow the interaction model, but it presents device design as following user behavior rather than framing the two as co-evolving.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we started with the software and let it teach us what the hardware should be. When you watch how people actually use ChatGPT, it's not like a search box. People talk to it the way they'd talk to a very smart friend who happens to be around all the time. They ask half-formed questions, they come back to the same thread for weeks, they use voice while they're walking or cooking. And almost none of that behavior was designed into the phone or the laptop. The phone is a device built around tapping on a glass rectangle, and you can feel the friction when you try to have a real conversation with an AI through it.

So the way I think about it is: the interaction pattern comes first, and the device should disappear into it. If the most natural thing is to just speak and be understood, and to have the system notice what's happening around you without you having to narrate it, then the right device probably isn't something you stare at. It's something that's more ambient, more aware of context, and much less demanding of your attention. The current generation of devices was built for a world where the computer couldn't understand you, so you had to do all the translation yourself. That constraint is gone now.

The other thing I'd say is that trust shows up in hardware in a way it doesn't in software. If a device is going to be with you all the time and really listening and seeing, people need to feel that it's on their side, that they understand what it's doing. That's partly a design problem and partly a company problem. So when we think about devices, we're thinking as much about how to earn that trust as about the form factor. The goal is something that feels calm, that makes you feel more present in your life rather than less, which is kind of the opposite of what most consumer technology has done for the last fifteen years.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT use patterns should guide device design, but presents that relationship as one-way; it does not clearly say the two co-evolve.

astra-6.text:
I think the way people interact with ChatGPT is a clue that we might want a different kind of device. The devices we have today were designed around clicking, typing, opening apps, and looking at a screen. And you can put AI into that experience, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what the experience should be if you start with AI.

If you can just say what you want, have a conversation, and trust the system to help you over time, that opens up a different set of design possibilities. Maybe the device can demand less of your attention. Maybe you don’t have to keep picking it up and navigating through things.

But I think you have to learn that from how people actually use these systems. The interaction informs the device, and then the device changes what kinds of interactions are possible. You develop those together.

r001.rationale: It says interaction informs device design, devices change possible interactions, and the two are developed together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way people interact with ChatGPT gives us a reason to rethink what a device should be. If you have to open an app, type a question, and wait for an answer, you’re fitting this new capability into a familiar interface. That’s useful, but it may not be the most natural way to interact with an AI.

The interesting design question is: what would you want the interaction to feel like? When should it listen, when should it respond, and when should it stay out of the way? Sometimes you want a screen and a lot of detail. Sometimes you just want to say something and get a short answer. I think the device should follow from those needs, and from what we learn about how people actually use the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says device design should follow interaction needs and observed use, but does not clearly describe device design and ChatGPT interactions as evolving together.
